This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel framework for modeling and forecasting count time series that exhibit both nonlinear mean and variance trends, as well as potential structural breaks. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach enables a low-order model to capture complex, non-linear dynamics in the mean and variance without requiring deterministic time-dependent parameters or seasonal dummy variables. The empirical analysis compares the new TV-PARX model against existing count time series models, highlighting its superior performance through model selection criteria, likelihood-based methods, and direct forecasting accuracy metrics. Furthermore, the study examines the model's dynamic dynamics, validates its dynamic forecasting capabilities, and analyzes the dynamic determinants driving these changes. The proposed methodology is made available as the rtvparx package in R. Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/RAM) telescope at Fairbanks, Alaska, and the HARPs (A, B, C, D) at Harbin, China, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Key strategies involve averaging photometry across a vast number of stars, applying rigorous quality controls, and utilizing advanced analysis methods. These approaches have also yielded benefits as a by-product, including better data quality, the identification of atmospheric emission sources, and the detection of subtle, temporally and spatialally varying seeing variations. Given the calibration-independent nature of this method, it offers an ideal tool for validating calibration-derived VAOD measurements from other instruments, such as AATAs, CRDs, and Bodines. Furthermore, because this technique is globally applicable, it holds significant potential for future space-based missions, including the proposed Light Curve Absorption Sensor (LCAS) on the Japanese PLATO (Planetary Transits and Oscilliations of stars) telescope. We conclude by outlining future directions for this method. This study evaluates and compares various integrators for the configurational Langevin dynamics (CD) required in sampling and analysis of equilibrium properties for configurational optimization and molecular simulation. Theoretical comparisons highlight the impact of time-step size and dimensionality on accuracy, while numerical experiments using toluene and C60 fullerene demonstrate the validity of these findings across a range of parameters. For C60, the study observes a significant reduction in the effective time-step when utilizing second- and higher-order schemes, ultimately limiting the efficiency gains from smaller timesteps. Consequently, the simple Euler method is identified as the optimal choice for CD sampling in both chemical and biological systems. It is further argued that the persistent myth regarding the unsuitability of Euler for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations stems from confusion between the larger timesteps feasible in classical (positional) momentum-based integrators and the smaller timesteps necessary for Langevin integrators, particularly for systems like C60 where high-frequency normal modes are present. Ultimately, for CD sampling, the Euler method offers the best balance of robustness and efficiency, outperforming second- and higher-order schemes by nearly an order of magnitude at practical timesteps, and remains superior even at smaller timesteps where higher-order methods show relative advantages. Given that CD sampling is increasingly utilized for biological systems to explore conformational spaces through techniques like simulated annealing, configurational optimization, and free energy calculations, the selection of an appropriate integrator is critical. The results confirm that Euler is the most suitable integrator for these applications, providing the greatest robustness and efficiency. Current automatic image description models are typically trained and assessed using crowdsourced human-generated captions, which are often selected from a dataset like COCO \cite{COCO} to serve as ground truth. The underlying assumption is that these references are flawless; however, as demonstrated in Figure 1, such data frequently contain errors, inconsistencies, and biases that can negatively impact the evaluation of systems like COCOEval, which rely on these flawed standards. This paper examines the issues inherent in reference data used for assessing automatic image descriptions, highlighting specific problems through examples. We propose that descriptive image captioning tasks should be reconceptualized as reference-free, end-to-end optimization problems. To support this approach, we introduce a new dataset, COCO-OSD, which collects over 120,000 open-ended descriptions per image from non-native English speakers. This dataset will enable the development of evaluation metrics aligned with end-to-end optimization goals. Furthermore, we define a set of criteria for "high-quality" references and present methods to identify and filter them out. Our findings indicate that approximately 20% of COCO captions do not meet these high-quality standards. Finally, we discuss potential applications of both optimized end-to-end evaluation methods and filtered reference datasets. The accompanying video demonstration is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U3p312111gE.  Our source code and data will be made publicly accessible.

Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past perturbative approaches. For Euclidean conformal field theories in two dimensions, we offer a novel, fully non-perturbative framework based on the expectation values of normal-ordered monomials of free scalar fields. Within this basis, complexity is determined by determining the most optimal unitary transformation. Leveraging the Euclidean conformal invariance, we derive a set of equations for this optimal transformation that relies solely on the theory's invariants, mirroring the Euler-Arnold equation used in control theory. By solving these equations for monomial orderings, we establish explicit non-perturbative formulas for complexity. When expressed in terms of Witten diagrams, these formulas reveal a striking structural similarity to the recently proposed "complexity from variance" framework in dual gravitational theories. Finally, for specific monomial orderings, our results align precisely with the conventional unitary circuit definition, providing the first evidence that such an equivalence holds non-perturbatively within a quantum field theory. Our findings support the feasibility of defining complexity via variance in dual two-dimensional Euclidean conformal field theories, even when unitary circuit constructions are not apparent. Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. Although not a fitting program itself, this framework serves as ideal preparation for any fitting suite, including xFitter \cite{XFitter}, CTU \cite{CTU}, AJETXS \cite{AJETX}, DoubleT \cite{DoubleT}, and others. As a standalone tool, it also stands as a significant asset for the CT-UXS (Consultant Teager - University Extra Small) family of Parton Distribution functions. This document describes the theory fitting framework, and when combined with the experimental data integration layer, constitutes the complete CT-UXS fitting project. Additionally, we briefly outline the data integration layer, which remains outside the scope of this work. We have implemented and tested this framework within the CT-UXS project using XFitter \cite{XFitter} as the external fitter, and the approach is universally applicable to other fitting projects and initiatives. The core concept involves decomposing the prediction process for each dataset into discrete, reusable steps (see Fig. \ref{fig:process}), which are then orchestrated by "recipes" that assemble these steps into a linear workflow specific to each dataset. These recipes are defined in YAML files, offering a clear and maintainable configuration method.

This study employs Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) to examine how a turbulent methane-air jet flame reacts to transverse acoustic forcing within a compressible, linearly sheared planar jet. The research begins by validating a linearized model against the DNS data in the near-field, demonstrating that this simplified model accurately predicts reaction rates without requiring the detailed dynamics of the actual flow. Subsequently, the work identifies an optimal forcing frequency that maximizes reaction rate fluctuations in the near-field, which aligns with the frequency exhibiting the largest amplitude in the DNS spectra. Finally, the linearized model is utilized to analyze reaction rate fluctuations across a wide range of frequencies, regardless of their initial amplitude. Under conditions of strong acoustic velocity perturbations (M0 = 0.2), the study reveals that vortex formation and the resulting trapping of fluid strips drive fluctuations at low frequencies. Conversely, at higher frequencies, fluctuations are dominated by acoustic resonance, with standing wave patterns emerging both globally and within individual fluid elements. Finally, within the linear regime, the influence of Reynolds number (Re) on reaction rate fluctuations at the dominant resonant frequency is investigated, showing that these fluctuations increase as Re decreases due to a shift in the dominant frequency toward lower values. Ultimately, this work provides the first comprehensive characterization of reaction rate fluctuations in a turbulent jet flame under linearized acoustic forcing, achieved through the development of a novel modeling framework. This approach decouples spatial inhomogeneities caused by mean velocity shear from oscillations induced by acoustic forcing, offering a versatile tool for investigating flame responses to complex, time-dependent acoustic perturbations in the linear regime. Furthermore, this linearized model serves as an essential component for a forthcoming study that extends analysis into the nonlinear regime using an active flame methodology.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal constitutive relation directly connects the torsionless, metric-compatible, historical-dependent connection (representing the gravitational field) to the matter distribution (energy-momentum tensor), utilizing the classical, instantaneous Riemannian tetrad as an intermediary. Through this reformulation, it becomes evident that a nonlocal, metric-compatible tetrad constitutes the fundamental gravitational variable in NLG, analogous to how the electric displacement serves as the fundamental variable in nonlocal electrodynamics. The study derives this constitutive relation for NLG and evaluates several existing models. Furthermore, it demonstrates that, under specific assumptions, a Born-Infeld type nonlocal constitutive relation for gravity can be derived from recent observational data concerning the acceleration of cosmic expansion.

This presentation reports on selected results from ultra-small systems at LHC energies, covering both ALICE and Atlas experiments. The discussion begins with a review of recent findings on collective phenomena in these systems, followed by an analysis of strangeness enhancement. It then moves on to examine the validity of hydrodynamic descriptions and the application of chemical freeze-out models at ultra-sparse energies. Finally, the talk addresses the onset of partonic saturation within these systems. All discussions are grounded in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, where small systems exhibit many striking characteristics that mirror those observed in larger systems. These features often suggest the emergence of quark-gluon plasma, although definitive proof remains elusive. Consequently, small systems at LHC energies represent a compelling area of research. The accompanying report highlights specific results supporting this narrative, though it is by necessity non-comprehensive and selective in scope. A primary motivation for this focus is the growing volume of data generated by small-system studies at both LHC and future colliders, which demands systematic organization. Additionally, the rise of machine learning has enabled the identification of quark-gluon plasma signatures in small systems through the analysis of massive datasets, a topic also briefly covered herein. Overall, this work provides a structured overview of collective behavior in ultra-small systems at LHC energies, emphasizing that such systems display numerous phenomena typically associated with larger heavy-ion collisions. These observations continue to fuel vigorous debates regarding the physics underlying these events. While this report does not delve into the specifics of those debates, it serves as an introduction to a special issue of Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics dedicated to small systems at LHC and future collider energies, compiled by a global community of experts in this field. The special issue begins with a comprehensive review of small systems at LHC and future colliders, followed by thirteen articles exploring various aspects of this research area. Readers are directed to the introduction for further details regarding the contents of this special issue. The collection of articles in this special issue is not accessible via DOI; access is possible only through the links provided in this abstract.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. These findings indicate that the millisecond neutron stars in the Galactic Centre likely belong to a population of systems capable of operating below the threshold of current X-ray telescopes, such as the so-called "ofat" systems, without requiring the introduction of black holes into every possible Galactic Centre neutron star configuration.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two distinct sets of entities, a structure that is especially valuable for identifying hidden relationships between separate groups of items. This process, known as bipartiteization, is essential for constructing such graphs from non-bipartite data. A specific technique for achieving this involves vertex splitting, where subdivided paths replace split vertices. Although existing methods cover all possible subdivision patterns, they are computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale graphs. This study introduces a comprehensive approach to bipartiteization that minimizes the number of edges required, ensuring an optimal edge-subdivided bipartite representation. For complete graphs, this aligns with earlier findings indicating that the minimum edges needed correspond to a squared relationship with the original graph's size. We present a algorithm determines the optimal subdivision pattern for each vertex to achieve the most efficient optimal edge-subdivided bipartite graph. Relying on a characteristic subset of vertices called a module, our method systematically assigns a specific subdivision type to every vertex within this subset, while treating vertices outside it uniformly. As a result, the problem reduces to finding the ideal subdivision for the unused vertices. By employing dynamic programming on the complement of a maximum matching within a complete bipartite graph, we derive an closed-form expression for the optimal subdivision of a pair of vertices based on their degree. Finally, we validate the correctness of our algorithm through theoretical analysis and demonstrate the accuracy of the closed-form solution using both theoretical arguments and empirical data. Furthermore, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm to calculate optimal subdivision patterns for individual vertices within a real-world dataset. Our implemented algorithm processes a book trading graph comprising 10,000 publishers and 10,000 authors in under a second, yielding a simplified bipartite structure with approximately 300,000 fewer edges than previous methods. The resulting graph is visualized in the accompanying video. Ultimately, this optimal edge-subdivided model serves as a powerful tool for analyzing and working with non-bipartite datasets. Our implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ChetanGupta1997/Bipartiteizing_Complete_Graphs_. We conclude by outlining several open challenges related to these graphs and their potential applications. Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks, enabling the extraction of secret information at speeds unattainable by attacks alone. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method for degrading CPU performance through a combination of current limiting, power capping, and microarchitectural flushing. Unlike previous approaches that focused on single-core isolation, HyperDegrade utilizes microarchitectural side channels to degrade a target core's performance without requiring physical performance isolation between cores. Evaluations using a high-frequency core demonstrate that HyperDegrade can reduce the target core's effective performance by factors exceeding 10x, with finer-grained degradation levels also achievable. The findings indicate that the effectiveness of performance degradation is limited by the CPU's cache size and cache line width. When assessed from the perspective of side-channel attacks, HyperDegrade offers a more effective alternative to traditional methods for specific scenarios. Furthermore, when evaluated against current state-of-the-art performance degradation techniques in the context of HyperDegrade's underlying principles, it achieves superior performance without introducing the associated drawbacks. Finally, in the context of performance degradation side-channels, HyperDegrade stands out as the most effective technique for our specific evaluations, delivering the strongest results without the negative consequences found in other methods. Our evaluations confirm that the efficacy of performance degradation depends on the microarchitectural characteristics of the target CPU, and that HyperDegrade provides the best outcomes for our specific microarchitectural configurations.

An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Our findings indicate that the unknotting number, Delta-move distance, Sharp-move distance, and Gamma-move distance are interrelated within the context of classical knots and visibly realizable welded knots. For instance, the unknotting distance over classical unknotting operations (such as the crossing change) is always greater than or equal to the unknotting distance via the diagonal move. Conversely, for the specific knot 9_4, its unknotting number is 3, yet its unknotting distance measured by the diagonal move is 4. Finally, we establish that the invariant |Alex - Alex+| (where Alex and Alex+ represent the Alexander invariants for the classical unknot and a nontrivial visibly realizable welded knot, respectively) is a invariant for the diagonal move in the domain of welded knots. Consequently, the unknotting distance of certain nontrivial visibly realizable welded knots exceeds their unknotting number when calculated using diagonal moves. Our results highlight that the set of unknotting operations for classical knots is strictly contained within that of diagonal moves, which in turn is strictly contained within the set of unknotting operations for welded knots: Unknotting operations (classical) $\subset$ Unknotting operations (diagonal) $\subset$ Unknotting operations (welded). Coordination represents a fundamental capability for multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become non-affine. Furthermore, we present an algorithm designed to compute a "best response" equilibrium and evaluate its performance. The results indicate that when the prior distribution lacks diffuseness, the best response equilibrium consistently outperforms the affine Nash equilibrium. These conclusions hold true even as the complexity of the priority task increases. To validate these theoretical discoveries, we conducted simulations using realistic parameters for both the prior distribution and environmental conditions, confirming that the best response equilibrium surpasses the affine Nash equilibrium in performance. Additionally, we observed that increasing the complexity of the prior distribution regarding task difficulty leads to improved performance for the best response equilibrium. Finally, we assessed the practical viability of implementing the best response equilibrium by comparing it against alternative coordination methods, such as random selection.

This paper demonstrates the embedding of regularly acting groups and diagonal groups into wreath products under their product action by utilizing Cartesian Decomposition. When combined with the embedding methods from Part I of reference [1], these techniques enable the embedding of a group's regular action into a wreath product's product action, as well as the embedding of its diagonal action (for a specific type of group), facilitating the embedding of a regularly acting group's action into a wreath product's product action. Consequently, this approach yields new results regarding the free products of embeddings for regularly acting groups. These findings are applied to prove that the free product of the special linear groups $SL(n,\mathbb{C})$ and $SL(n,\mathbb{H})$ (where $n\geq 3$) with the free group $F_{\mathbf{r}}$ ($\mathbf{r}\geq 1$) is 2-constrained. Additionally, the free products of the special linear groups $SL(n,\mathbb{C})$, $SL(n,\mathbb{H})$ ($n\geq 3$), and $SL(m,\mathbb{F})$ ($m\geq 2$, where $\mathbb{F}$ represents a finite field) with a hyperbolic-type Artin group are shown to be 2-constrained. The concepts of Cartesian Decomposition and 2-constrained groups are defined and examined within this work. It is important to note that these concepts, along with the techniques employed, are applicable to linear groups acting on finite sets and with Artin groups. Furthermore, these methods potentially offer a solution to the fixed point free conjugates problem for the specified types of groups. These approaches may also be useful for other problems involving regularly acting groups, such as the so-called "Kromhout Conjecture." Finally, the methods presented here could benefit other areas of mathematics, including the study of free products of groups, Artin groups, and related fields. The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors. By introducing a novel interferometer topology between the signal-recycling mirror and the main interferometer, we demonstrate that this high-frequency sensitivity can be surpassed. This new configuration, which resembles a Sagnac loop, is termed the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer. When integrated into a laser interferometric gravitational-wave detector, it forms a triply-coupled cavity known as the sloshing-Sagnac-cavity. We employ a quantum-optical master equation approach to analyze how losses in this cavity impact quantum fluctuations. Our results indicate that, despite the presence of losses, the sloshing-Sagnac-cavity enables the detection of strain fluctuations at frequencies higher than its own bandwidth. Furthermore, we find that tripling the optical path length in the signal-recycling cavity—without increasing optical power—can result in a total system loss of approximately 20 ppm while still achieving a tenfold improvement in high-frequency sensitivity compared to a conventional configuration. Using a 200-meter baseline detector as a reference, we project that a detector featuring one sloshing-Sagnac-cavity could improve the O3-level sensitivity by a factor of 2.5 at 2.5 kHz and by a factor of 3 at 1.5 kHz. We also provide general guidelines for optimizing such a detector's sensitivity. As an initial design concept, a detector incorporating a single sloshing-sagnac-cavity would offer superior sensitivity beyond the bandwidth of an additional sloshing-sagnac-cavity that could be added in future upgrades. Such an architecture would create a doubly-coupled sloshing-sagnac-cavity, functioning as a triply-coupled harmonic oscillator whose bandwidth would be determined by the optical losses of its constituent cavities. Our study suggests that, even with non-negligible losses, a 200-meter baseline detector equipped with this doubly-coupled cavity could reach a total loss of around 50 ppm while maintaining a bandwidth exceeding 2 kHz and achieving improved sensitivity relative to a standard triply-coupled detector at frequencies above 1 Hz. Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationary and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) visibility regions. These regions are a primary cause of access failures in random access protocols. Although prior research has extensively analyzed non-overlapping visibility regions (NOVR) to derive upper bounds on data rates, NOVR has not been a limiting factor in existing random access protocols, which have instead focused on the number of antennas within LoS regions. This paper examines the NOVR issue within the XL-MIMO random access protocol, demonstrating that NOVR significantly degrades data rates when UEs are located far from the array. We introduce a "closest-LoS UE" based XL-MIMO random access protocol and prove that its data rates remain unaffected by NOVR. Comparative data rate analyses between traditional NOVR-aware linear scaling strategies and our proposed protocol reveal that the latter offers data rate improvements of up to 10x. Finally, we introduce an optimized XL-MIMO random access protocol that integrates NOVR awareness with our proposed method, achieving data rate gains of 10% to 20%.

Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still deliver competitive results in many scenarios. Leveraging the superior representational power of neural networks, we explore the potential of an additive architecture where a final prediction is generated by a an $m$-gram model combined with a neural $M$-gram ($m \ge M$) model. We refer to this approach as residual $N$-gram language modeling. Extensive experiments on five standard datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms various existing $N$-gram and neural models. This study examines how state-of-the-art neuro-symbolic optical character recognition systems perform on ballot images to enable vote tabulation. This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Polar Earth System Model (PolaREM). The model incorporates simplified lateral boundary conditions and parameterized shallow convection, while friction is introduced through both linear drag and beta-effect drag to simulate interactions with surface features. Reproducing Earth-like wind speeds requires specific combinations of rheological parameters, radiative-forcing, and rotational rates. By systematically varying these factors, the research identifies distinct circulation regimes characterized by dominant balance forces: from geostrophic and cyclostrophic flows to turbulent and boundary layer regimes. A key finding is that friction is essential for generating Earth-like wind speeds in an Earth-like atmosphere; without it, turbulent and cyclostrophic regimes fail to achieve the necessary velocities. The study concludes with recommendations for representing topographic friction and surface-atmosphere drag in both simplified GCMs and climate models. Additionally, the research outlines a recommended sequence for incorporating complexity into global climate models, particularly regarding surface-atmosphere friction and topographic features. The governing equations, summarized circulation regimes as a function of rheological parameters and rotational rates, and identified optimal friction parameters for mimicking Earth's atmosphere are compiled into comprehensive tables. These tables and equations serve as a valuable reference for selecting appropriate friction parameters in simplified GCMs to match the characteristics of more advanced atmospheric models and real-world conditions. Furthermore, these tools offer utility for exoplanet atmospheres, where surface-atmosphere friction and topographic features can be inferred from rotational rates and atmospheric behaviors. Specifically, these elements can help determine topographic features and friction characteristics in extraterrestrial atmospheres lacking direct topographic data, as demonstrated in this work for an Earth-like atmosphere on a tidally locked exoplanet. These resources also support the interpretation of atmospheric characteristics from extraterrestrial atmospheres, such as Titan's, that have not yet been fully analyzed. Finally, these tools assist in establishing boundary conditions for studying atmospheric changes and their responses to perturbations in both Earth's and extraterrestrial atmospheres. For instance, these resources were utilized to explore how topographic-atmosphere friction influences vortex formation and evolution in an Earth-like atmosphere on a tidally locked exoplanet without magnetic field-induced barotropic instabilities.

This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. Finally, the paper reports on a regularized real integral representation of the $\Gamma$ function proposed by the authors, contrasting it with Srivastava et al.'s formulation. Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method. Our results demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns with existing quantum dynamics simulations across a range of initial conditions. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of quantum and thermal fluctuations, as well as gas interactions, on the simulation variance. Additionally, we derive a generalization of this linearized scheme applicable to arbitrary dimensions. When combined with the stochastic positive-P method, this work offers the most powerful classical simulation technique for quantum many-body systems still feasible. Finally, we extend this linearized formalism to address non-Gaussian non-equilibrium scenarios, and the resulting full positive-P and linearized schemes are compared under various initial conditions. While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically outline the processes of knowledge acquisition, construction, and optimization. Finally, we explore recent applications of these architectures in various scenarios and forecast future research directions. The comprehensive nature of this survey underscores the potential of Teacher-Student architectures to enable intelligent systems with both high efficiency and robust performance.   $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and establish an algebraic isomorphism between $R_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and
  $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Furthermore, we derive an explicit presentation for $R_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$
  involving generating relations and a Hilbert-style resolution of its

Significance testing, particularly the paired-permutation test, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN(\log G + \log N))$ time, where $G$ represents the number of data points (e.g., sentences or articles) in a single test instance and $N$ is the total number of instances in the dataset. Empirical results demonstrate that our exact algorithm is 100 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 10,000 samples on a real-world dataset. Additionally, the algorithm is 10 times quicker than a Monte Carlo approximation with 1,000 samples when performing the test on the dataset. As a byproduct, we present a concise exact algorithm for calculating the depth of a data distribution under the group of data-swap symmetry. Finally, we derive a new upper bound for the volume of the data distribution's orbit under the combined groups of data-swap and system-blind symmetries, which is crucial for the exact calculation of this volume. The exact paired-permutation test offers a more rigorous alternative to p-value-based significance testing for comparing the performance of two NLP systems. Adopting this test could lead to rewarding larger performance gains that were previously not statistically significant under common significance thresholds, such as $\pu{0.05}$. The source code and dataset required to replicate our empirical results are available at https://github.com/lingdina/ExactPairedPermutationTesting.

Using the AMPT multiphase transport model, we investigated the connection between initial geometric anisotropy and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Our results show that, unlike the elliptic flow $v_2$, the triangular flow $v_3$ exhibits minimal dependence on centrality. Once the influence of initial geometry is accounted for, the ratio $v_3/\epsilon_3$ rises with increasing transverse particle density, mirroring the behavior of $v_2/\epsilon_2$. Furthermore, the $p_T$ dependence of $v_3$ observed across all centralities aligns qualitatively with the dependence of $v_2$ on ellipticity $\epsilon_2$. These findings support the hydrodynamic framework for describing anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at this energy. Additionally, the $v_3$ values derived from our model agree well with recent measurements obtained via the three-party event plane method and the $\gamma$-conversion electron method in Au+Au collisions at the same centrality and energy.

This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that models target birth and undetected target intensities on a grid. It incorporates Poisson distributed stochastic super-Gaussian noise into the mean of a multi-Bernoulli component, utilizing a mean-field approximation for the PMBM density to derive a point-globally optimal fixed-grid birth Monte Carlo sampler. Simulations demonstrate that this method outperforms conventional PMBM samplers in scenarios involving undetected targets and low detection probabilities, offering significant advantages for sensor management systems. The simulations also highlight the practical value of the novel sampler for real-world implementations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first explicit formulation of a point-globally optimal fixed-grid birth model for PMBM. Potential applications extend beyond sensor management to areas like search and rescue operations. Further details are available at: http://arxiv.org/abs/2009.01260. Codes can be accessed at: https://github.com/chenyuheng98/PMBM_with_partially_global_birth.

Soccer is a game characterized by sparse rewards, where even minor strategic errors in pivotal moments can alter the match outcome. Although soccer serves as a classic example of a multi-agent partial observable Markov decision process, existing research has predominantly focused on standard contexts, often neglecting the unique challenges posed by critical scenarios. These high-stakes situations include one-vs-one confrontations during penalties, corner kicks, throw-ins, and goal kick scenarios. To address this, we introduce a novel state representation and a two-phase training approach for soccer games using deep reinforcement learning. Our methodology enables the agent to select optimized actions, particularly during these critical moments. Specifically, the first phase trains an optimal policy for standard scenarios, while the second phase focuses exclusively on critical situations, conditioned on the policy generated from the first. Validation was conducted via simulations and real-world soccer data, with results indicating that the agent's decisions align closely with those made by human professionals in these pivotal events. Furthermore, when applied to real data, the optimized actions derived from the second phase demonstrate that teams can achieve higher expected goals ($xG$) and scores by adopting these strategies; for instance, the recommended post-corner kick actions increased the attacking team's $xG$ by 1.2% and their winning probability by 0.1%. Ultimately, this work provides insights into optimal behaviors during critical soccer scenarios, offering actionable recommendations for both professional players and coaches. Driven by the recent surge in telework and remote work arrangements, there is now significant interest in controlling complex systems from a distance. This study demonstrates that a single-point Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) system can be operated remotely to generate two-dimensional (2D) vibration contour maps. While this approach does not replace the need for a 2D LDV system for specific applications, it offers a viable solution when such specialized equipment is unavailable. To implement this, we developed a system where the LDV's light source and detector are adjusted manually at the start, after which all other operations are managed remotely. The resulting 2D vibration maps were acquired using a single-point LDV (Model: OFV-5000) coupled with a single-mode fiber, measured on the air-coupled (1,0) Lamb wave mode on an aluminum plate. These results confirm that a single-point LDV system can be controlled remotely to capture 2D vibration data, providing a practical alternative when 2D LDV hardware is not accessible. This work was created by the authors to address these specific constraints. Additionally, the single-point LDV system described here was utilized to characterize the vibration modes of a simply supported square plate, aiming to identify an optimal excitation location for effective mode shaping. This final application was developed in response to a specific requirement for controlling vibration modes on a tailored simply supported square plate. Further details regarding this application can be found in the corresponding manuscript: Remote Operation of a Single-Point LDV System for 2D Measurement and Vibration Mode Shaping on a Simply Supported Square Plate. We derive the spectral and orbital stability of the harmonic and higher-order solitary wave solutions for the one-dimensional Klein--Gordon equation, which is coupled to an anharmonic oscillator through its boundary, using a combination of operator theoretic approaches and spectral analysis for constant coefficient differential operators with an anharmonic potential. For this system, we establish a correspondence between orbital stability and spectral (and hence operator) theoretic properties, demonstrating that both concepts depend solely on the spectral characteristics of the linearized operator. Consequently, our operator theoretic framework provides a comprehensive description of the spectrum, revealing no unexpected spectral properties arise from the anharmonic term in the potential. Finally, our methodology for addressing spectral and orbital stability is versatile and can be applied to other problems involving boundary coupled PDEs, such as the wave equation coupled to the Schrödinger equation.

This paper offers a qualitative examination of potentially flawed outputs generated by contextualized embedding-based techniques for identifying diachronic semantic change. We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is questionable. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual frequency, a bias inherent to their distributional nature that differs from issues seen in static embedding methods. Furthermore, these models often blend syntactic and semantic features of lexical items. Finally, we suggest several potential future solutions to address these problems. The detailed linguistic insights gained from our study will prove valuable for developing more effective diachronic semantic change detection methods and enhancing lexicographic resources. Our code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/Noaam/GOLD. Ultimately, our findings suggest that evaluating AI for change detection requires a nuanced, expert-driven linguistic assessment rather than relying solely on traditional information-retrieval metrics like precision, recall, and F1 scores. Specifically, we observe that "gold" standards constructed by non-experts, whether by humans or machines, may inadvertently reinforce the very biases we aim to overcome in both existing techniques and future lexicographic resources.

The masses and spins of black holes powering Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) and producing jets or variability can be measured through the correlation between spin and X-ray/tidal properties. These spin determinations rely on physical mechanisms that generate X-ray variability or jets, which in turn are linked to the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). While a minimum spin value ($a_{\rm min}$) is required to explain these phenomena, the actual spin at this lower limit remains uncertain. If a specific mass range of black holes exists where a particular ultralight boson can form a cloud around the black hole via the superradiance mechanism, preventing the boson mass from exceeding the corresponding upper bound, the $a_{\rm min}$ for that mass range will be determined by the upper limit of the ultralight boson's mass within that range. By analyzing the spins of 27 $M\sim$ few$-$100 $M_{\odot}$ QNars (QSOs with narrow emission lines) and 17 $M\sim$ few$-$1000 $M_{\odot}$ BHVs (black hole variable frequency QSOs), we find that two complex scalar (or vector) bosons with masses $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\times10^{-11} M_{\odot}$ and $2.5^{+1.0}_{-0.7}\times10^{-11} M_{\odot}$ are disfavoured by the data at more than $95\%$ and $99\%$ confidence levels, respectively. Additionally, we examine the implications of this method for detecting ultralight bosons through future observations of less massive black holes.

Additionally, we determined the ground state energy through imaginary time integration. To verify our Monte Carlo results, we compared them against exact solutions derived for the ground state energy and various correlation functions. We introduce a variant of the quantum relational Hoare logic from Unruh (POPL 2019) that incorporates "expectations" into pre- and postconditions, enabling quantitative reasoning about pairs of quantum programs. Specifically, this logic allows for the verification of invariants, correctness, and correctness under a failure model. The integration of expectations facilitates the formulation and automation of composition, interference, and failure-model correctness rules, which are otherwise complex to define manually. Furthermore, under specific invariants and correctness criteria, the system supports automation for lifting, deterministic refinement, and monotonicity rules. The validity of all compositionality rules within this logic with expectations is established by induction on its syntax, a process supported by meta-theorems that generalize the induction hypothesis. While the core focus is on compositionality, the study also examines soundness regarding the failure model and an asymptotic model of correctness, ultimately demonstrating that the asymptotic model is strictly stronger than the failure model. The implementation of this quantum relational hoare logic with expectations serves as the foundation for a proof assistant designed to automate proofs of program invariants, correctness, and correctness within the failure model for pairs of quantum programs.

This study addresses the bias—defined as over- or underestimation—in the line-of-sight (LOS) velocity measurement errors ($\sigma_{\rm LOS}$) of vector magnetic field data used for solar vector imaging (SVI) spectral inversion. While current uncertainty estimation methods in spectral inversion rely on standard assumptions, these may not align with the actual precision achievable during the fitting process, particularly when inversion goals are ambitious. To tackle this issue, we developed a novel framework for estimating $\rm LOS$ velocity measurement errors that incorporates the specific objectives of each inversion. Utilizing this approach, we examined SDO/HSRP AIA 170\AA\ images and the VSHARP dataset to evaluate how $\sigma_{\rm LOS}$ bias influences the vertical ($B_z$) and transverse ($B_{\perp}$) magnetic field estimates in VSHARP. Our results indicate that reducing $\rm LOS$ velocity measurement noise by a factor of two would decrease $B_{\perp}$ error by approximately 15\%. Furthermore, we implemented a regularization technique within our new $\sigma_{\rm LOS}}$ estimation method to mitigate the associated bias, a strategy that could be adapted for other solar image processing tasks influenced by this data bias. By clarifying the link between $\rm LOS$ velocity measurement uncertainty and $B_{\perp}$ error, our work offers valuable insights for interpreting $B_{\perp}$ error bars in existing solar magnetic field datasets and for setting appropriate error bars in new datasets, ultimately aiding the effective utilization of vector magnetic field data in solar science. To facilitate this, we have made a Python package capable of estimating both the original and regularized $\rm LOS$ velocity measurement errors for spectral inversion data available at https://github.com/ruirui0102/Regularized_LOS_noise. This tool will support the characterization of $B_{\perp}}$ error in future solar vector magnetic field datasets. For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, we define the boolean complex of involutions as a counterpart to the boolean complex of $W$ investigated by Batzies and Knauer. We demonstrate that this complex is $(n-2)$-connected, where $n$ represents the count of positive involutions within $W$. Furthermore, we establish that the boolean complex of involutions for a finite Coxeter group is simply connected and possesses the homotopy type of a sphere, whereas for an affine Weyl group, it is an infinite dimensional contractible space. This study demonstrates that certain biharmonic hypersurfaces described by specific recurrent operators cannot exist within Euclidean space. Furthermore, it establishes that biharmonic hypersurfaces with the recurrent Ricci tensor in the Euclidean space must be minimal. The research also confirms that biharmonic hypersurfaces featuring the recurrent Hessian operator in Euclidean space require constant mean curvature; additionally, it proves that such hypersurfaces with the recurrent Weyl curvature operator cannot exist in Euclidean space. For any rational number $p/q$, numeration in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $A_p=\{0,1,...,p-1\}$ to rational values. The image of this function is denoted by $N_{p/q}$. While $N_{p/q}$ encompasses all nonnegative integers, existing literature typically concentrates on the subset of words evaluating to these integers; this set forms a context-free language over $A_{p/q}$, which is infinite and thus lacks a finite automaton representation. In contrast, we investigate the recognition of $N_{p/q}$ itself by finite automata operating on reversed words, or equivalently, by the set of context-free grammars that generate it. Specifically, we establish that a finite automaton (deterministic or nondeterministic) can recognize $N_{p/q}$ if and only if a regular language over $A_{p/q}$ corresponds to the digits of nonnegative integers representable in base $p/q$ using exclusively digits from $\{0,1,...,\max(0,-q)\}$. Furthermore, over the alphabet $A_{p/q}$, we define the $(p/q)$-integer relation as the most comprehensive context-free grammar (always deterministic) capable of generating all nonnegative integers representable in base $p/q$ as a sequence of digits from $\{0,1,...,p-1\}$. We demonstrate that this relation is precisely the regular language comprising all such valid digit sequences. Finally, we introduce the concept of a $p/q$-recognisable set of integers and show that an integer set is $p/q$-recognisable exactly when a corresponding set of nonnegative integers is regular over base $p/q$; we provide examples of sets that are 2/1-recognisable but not 3/1-recognisable. The notion of $p/q$-recognisability generalizes both regularity and context-freeness, and we conclude by outlining several of its fundamental properties.

Subsequently, in 1938, Menger asked whether a similar "anglemetric" could be derived from an angle space by defining angular separation instead of Euclidean distance between points. At that time, he also noted that solving these problems would be straightforward within the context of Hilbert spaces. This paper addresses these issues by establishing the existence of anglemetric spaces and demonstrating how to convert them into Carathéodory spaces (specifically, semimetric spaces satisfying the strict triangle inequality) that model actual angles. Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved significant success and are extensively utilized in safety-critical domains, including Lidar recognition systems for autonomous vehicles. Nevertheless, these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks designed to deceive predictions through stealthy semantic transformations like rotation and tapering. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing framework that delivers tight and scalable robustness guarantees for point cloud models against such attacks. We begin by classifying common 3D transformations into three groups: additive (e.g., shearing), composable (e.g., rotation), and indirectly composable (e.g., tapering), offering generic robustness certification strategies for each category. Subsequently, we define specialized certification protocols for various specific semantic transformations and their combinations. Extensive experiments on multiple common 3D transformations demonstrate that TPC significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods; for instance, our framework increases certified accuracy against twisting transformations along the z-axis (within 20°) from 20.1% to 81.1%. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/PointCloud-Robustness-Working-Group/TPC-Smoothing.

The verification techniques of formal methods are now being applied to program testing, with the goal of enhancing the reliability of software development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing serves as the testing counterpart to the geometric theory of verification that has gained significant traction recently. This theory demonstrates that, to achieve comprehensive coverage, random testing must be replaced with structured strategies such as context-oriented, variable-oriented, or hybrid approaches. Furthermore, coverage-driven testing can be made cost-effective through selective execution, optimized test suites, and prioritization. Finally, our coverage metrics enable end-to-end quality guarantees, ensuring that quality improvements occur throughout the trace of a program's lifecycle, which spans compilation, testing, development, deployment, and updates. To enable these capabilities, we have created an end-to-end environment known as GEt (the environment for Geometric Theory for Testing), which functions similarly to the F* environment for verification. We illustrate the practical value and benefits of our end-to-end coverage metrics and structured testing strategies by addressing the challenge of achieving thorough coverage in regression testing for evolved code. Additionally, we report on initial empirical findings regarding the effectiveness of prioritized, coverage-oriented regression testing in this context. The source code for GEt and related materials are accessible at https://github.com/GeometricMethods/Get-Gotc.

This paper presents an explicit formulation of the weight component of Serre's conjecture for GL_2, derived through Kummer theory without relying on the existence of modular forms. The approach utilizes the characteristic polynomial of a suitable lift of a Euclidean embedding of the Galois group of the underlying field. By applying this explicit formulation, the authors verify Carling's recent counterexample and provide a unified proof of the weight components of Serre's conjecture for both p-Euler characteristic lifts and their generalizations. Additionally, this explicit formulation serves as a crucial component in the proof of the full conjecture along Chebotarev dense sets within the work by the first author and W. Zhang [10]. The derivation of a precise version of Serre's conjecture on the existence of lifts along Galois dense sets is achieved via the method outlined in the collaboration between the first author and Zhang [11]. Furthermore, this explicit formulation enables a proof of the fact that the conjectured weight corresponds to the minimal extension of a character of Frobenius elements, as established by the first author in [8]. Alongside the application by the first author and Zhang [10], this paper represents the initial use of this explicit formulation outside the context of the proof for GL_2; consequently, it may facilitate analogous applications in other mathematical areas. The collaboration between the first author and A. Moulin-Sector on utilizing this explicit formulation for a counterexample to a conjecture by Momose and Yamaeda is detailed in [9].

Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, size, or shape evolution. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex damage patterns including delaminations that are difficult to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage shapes from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, specifically detecting through-hole and deliberate delamination defects. Additionally, we examined the reconstruction of natural delamination shapes occurring during through-hole damage events. The results indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based inversion methods such as EIT yields only limited accuracy for precise shape and size reconstruction. However, by incorporating a physics-based model and a genetic algorithm, our team successfully achieved accurate reconstruction of artificial through-holes, artificial delaminations, and natural damage shapes arising from through-hole events.

We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes geometric vectors, validating the decomposition of any vector into radial and angular components. Within this approach, we define two second-rank tensors: the metric tensor $g$ and the "angular" tensor $h$, which are mutually invertible. The tensor $h$ induces an inner product on the subspace of vectors orthogonal to the radial direction, effectively generating an induced metric on the unit sphere. Consequently, the pair $(g,h)$ functions analogously to the metric and area elements in integral formulations. Leveraging this formalism, we systematically derive a set of identities involving vector, matrix, and determinant operations, many of which are directly applicable in statistical physics, particularly when performing integrations over the unit sphere. To demonstrate the utility of these identities, we explicitly calculate the Gaussian integral of the determinant of a matrix of Gaussian-vector variables. Additionally, we apply this framework to derive a decomposition of the heat kernel for a free particle moving along a geodesic on the $n$-dimensional sphere $S^n$. Finally, we extend this method to compute the heat kernel for the spherical harmonic oscillator on $S^n$. Ultimately, we conclude that the $(g,h)$ tensor formalism serves as a valuable tool for performing integrations over the unit sphere. This paper also collects standard identities related to vector, trace, determinant, and Gaussian integrations specifically for Euclidean spaces.

Contextual linear bandits represent a theoretically significant model with extensive practical applications, recently attracting considerable attention in wireless networks where communication constraints have been a primary focus. In distributed settings, existing approaches predominantly rely on deterministic deterministic learning protocols, where agents transmit deterministic summaries of their context-limited loss functions to a central learner for policy optimization. This paper introduces a novel stochastic learning-inference protocol enabling efficient learning in distributed contextual linear bandits, even when loss functions remain local and contexts are unpredictable. Specifically, local agent contexts are utilized to infer loss characteristics, which are then inferred centrally to optimize the policy. Focusing on distributed wireless networks, we establish new lower bounds for linear inference, policy optimization, and the overall contextual linear bandit problem in distributed scenarios. These findings confirm that our proposed protocol achieves optimal efficiency in linear inference and near-optimality in both loss optimization and bandit performance within distributed contexts. As a byproduct, we demonstrate that traditional deterministic learning methods in distributed contextual linear bandits suffer from sub-optimality due to inherent information loss. Application to wireless networks is discussed as a final contribution. The core innovations of this work include the identification of information loss as a critical bottleneck in distributed contextual linear bandits, the development of a new stochastic protocol that overcomes this limitation, and the derivation of tight lower bounds that validate the optimality of the proposed approach. These results offer valuable insights for addressing information constraints in other distributed systems, such as recommendation engines, ad tech, and personalized search, where contexts are often unpredictable and loss functions are local. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor of five. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system.

Recently, industry applications of neural networks, particularly in computer vision, have increasingly utilized global average pooling (GAP) as a standard layer for feature extraction before feeding into fully connected layers. This paper demonstrates that dynamic backdoors can be made even more compact by incorporating the GAP layer into the activation function of the trigger itself. Our experimental results show that integrating the trigger's GAP layer into the trigger region successfully creates a more compact dynamic backdoor across various image sizes and architectures. These findings indicate that existing security countermeasures, which assume static backdoors, may be insufficient against such sophisticated dynamic exploits. This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. While Random Walk (RW)-based methods offer a promising alternative to bypass this bottleneck, they struggle with data heterogeneity, resulting in biased models. Conversely, standard FL algorithms manage data heterogeneity effectively but are limited by communication constraints. The proposed Random Walk for Learning (W4L) framework integrates both approaches to overcome limitations related to both bottlenecks and heterogeneity. The framework comprises two phases: an exploration phase utilizing RW to generate a data map, and a learning phase where a learning protocol is selected based on this map. Extensive simulations demonstrate that W4L surpasses existing RW and FL methods across various scenarios, effectively mitigating communication bottlenecks and handling data heterogeneity. Additional findings reveal that the proposed protocol achieves linear scaling of learning accuracy with respect to the number of iterations, outperforming traditional FL approaches. Simulation results also indicate that the initial data map significantly influences learning performance, with the greedy method yielding superior outcomes in most cases. To optimize this, a simple yet effective graph-based algorithm is introduced to automatically select the best learning strategy. Furthermore, real-world simulations based on image data confirm the framework's practical applicability. From an security perspective, the exploration phase requires access to the data graph; however, this can be managed via public metadata or a minimal data sample, rendering the framework applicable even when full data visibility is unavailable. Learning from data distributed over graphs represents a novel research area with significant potential, and this study offers theoretical insights and simulation-based validations supporting these conclusions. The proposed random walk-based framework provides a robust solution for overcoming communication bottlenecks and managing data heterogeneity in FL, with broad implications for applications such as medical imaging, where raw data transfer is often infeasible. At the heart of quantum nonlocality lie the phenomena of EPR steering, entanglement, and nonlocality, which form a strict hierarchy with nonlocality being the most extreme. We demonstrate that observing single-particle entanglement enables EPR steering, thereby placing it directly on the nonlocal side of the steering/nonlocal divide. Consequently, single-particle entanglement facilitates genuinely nonlocal effects, a finding we illustrate using a variant of the Grainy Light Nonlocality (GLN) experiment. Furthermore, we show that these outcomes also occur in a genuinely single-particle GLN setup. These results imply that, contrary to common belief, EPR steering does not represent the weakest form of nonlocality; indeed, specific types of single-particle entanglement are required to produce it. This conclusion holds regardless of the underlying quantum theory, the dimensions of Hilbert spaces, or the number of measurement settings or states employed. As a final application, we provide evidence that certain aspects of Bohmian trajectories are themselves nonlocal when derived from single-particle entangled states.

Although the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with advanced information technology systems has yielded substantial benefits in Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation techniques have become essential for IoV systems. However, these methods are often computationally expensive and may fail to fully guarantee privacy. In contrast, learning frameworks powered by emerging technologies like Blockchain and Distributed Learning have emerged as promising alternatives for enhancing data privacy in IoVs. Meanwhile, the concept of Federated Learning (FL), a distributed approach, has gained significant traction recently for ensuring data privacy and security. Yet, the introduction of FL has given rise to new vulnerabilities and threats within the IoV environment. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application of FL systems supported by Blockchain within IoVs, specifically examining FL architectures, Blockchain-supported mechanisms, IoV-specific challenges, and potential solutions. Furthermore, this review identifies existing gaps and proposes future research directions for Blockchain- and Blockchain-inspired supported FL frameworks in IoVs. Ultimately, this work aims to offer a detailed examination of how Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning can address privacy and security concerns in IoVs. The findings are summarized in the table of contents and Figure 1, with a list of acronyms and abbreviations provided at the end of this introduction. Our survey is structured as follows: Section 2 offers an overview of IoV and FL; Section 3 details the FL architecture supported by Blockchain in IoVs; Section 4 categorizes various Blockchain-supported mechanisms for data privacy in IoVs; Section 5 discusses FL-specific challenges in IoVs; Section 6 explores solutions to these challenges; Section 7 reviews existing threats and vulnerabilities in Blockchain- and Blockchain-inspired supported FL frameworks; Section 8 outlines future research directions; and finally, Section 9 concludes the paper.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks widely employed for sequence analysis and classification. Despite their success, LSTMs demand substantial computational resources, which restricts the deployment of state-of-the-art architectures in memory-constrained environments, particularly when processing high-dimensional data like video. This paper presents an algorithm and hardware co-design approach for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTMs optimized for video recognition tasks. Our method introduces a hardware-friendly hierarchical Tucker (HT) decomposition that preserves accuracy while revealing non-trivial algorithmic and hardware-level insights for efficient LSTM implementation. At the algorithmic level, we segment the LSTM matrix-weight tensors into sub-tensors and apply the HT decomposition specifically to these weight sub-tensors. On the hardware front, we designed a high-performance, area-efficient HT-specific accelerator. Leveraging the unique structure of HT tensors, this accelerator executes multi-dimensional core tensor $\times$ Tucker tensor contraction without converting the Tucker tensor into a sparse format, thereby offering significant advantages over conventional sparse LIMS (Look-Up Memory based Inference) engines for HT-specific workloads. Validations via simulations, FPGA prototypes, and GPU-accelerated simulations demonstrate that our HT decomposition maintains high accuracy, and the proposed LIMS+HT architecture delivers superior performance and energy efficiency for video recognition. Compared to a state-of-the-art area-efficient LSTM hardware design, our HT-based architecture achieves a 2.77$\times$ improvement in performance per area (PPA) and a 3.25$\times$ gain in operations per second per milliwatt ($\text{Sec}/\text{mW}$) when operating at 200 MHz. Furthermore, our HT-based design outperforms existing hardware solutions by orders of magnitude in both performance and energy efficiency across various video datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this HT-based LIMS+HT architecture represents the first implementation for linalg-based inference on HT-specific workflows. The accompanying open-source algorithmic and hardware designs are available at: https://github.com/HTLIMS/HTLIMS-Architecture-and-Design.

This paper examines the Schrödinger equation featuring a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^{d}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up from Theorems H and I in [10] by applying a concentration compactness/rigidity argument adapted from the work of Merle and Viéville [19]. Merle and Viéville [10] originally proved that orbital stability and global existence fail when the nonlinearity is mass-supercritical and the obstacle's geometry is strictly convex. Consequently, in the exterior domains associated with strictly convex obstacles, the nonlinearity remains "effectively" supercritical even if it is mass-subcritical and the boundary is merely $C^{3}$ smooth. Our primary technical advancement involves proving a reflection phenomenon for high-energy solutions within a "near-ground state" energy regime, occurring when the solution blows up along a geodesic that reflects off the boundary. This phenomenon arises because, at the moment of reflection, the solution exhibits a "near-blow-up" characteristic typical of ground state solutions, as illustrated in Figure 1.
